title: Juwayriyyah's freed people
hookLine: a captive comes to ask for help with her freedom, and her marriage sets her people free (Abu Dawud)

lines: SHE CAN'T PAY FOR HER FREEDOM.
cards: A battle is over, and the losing tribe's people are captives. Among them is the daughter of their chief. She has made an agreement to buy her own freedom, and she can't pay it.

So she does something brave: she goes straight to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to ask for help. Aisha, watching her come to the door, tells us in Abu Dawud's collection what happened next.

teach.h: SHE TELLS HIM WHO SHE IS.
teach.b: The tribe was the Banu al-Mustaliq, and the woman was Juwayriyyah, daughter of their chief, al-Harith.

In the report, she tells the Prophet plainly who she is, what has happened to her, and that she needs help paying for her freedom. He offers her something better: he will pay what she owes and marry her. She accepts.
Then comes the part the story is really about. The news goes around the camp: the Prophet has married Juwayriyyah.

teach.h: HOW CAN WE HOLD HIS IN-LAWS?
teach.b: And the companions, who were holding her people as captives, said, in effect: these are now the Prophet's in-laws. How can we keep his relatives as captives? And they let them go.
The report counts it: through that marriage, a hundred households of the Banu al-Mustaliq were set free.
Then Aisha adds a sentence of her own: she knew of no woman who was a greater blessing to her people than Juwayriyyah. One woman walked in to ask about her own freedom. Her people walked out free.
Look at the chain. Her courage to ask. His answer, larger than the question.
And then the companions, who weren't commanded to do anything, choosing on their own to free people because of a new family tie. Honor for one person spread outward until it became freedom for many.

One more glimpse: Sahih Muslim has Juwayriyyah sitting in her place of prayer from dawn until the late morning, remembering Allah. The woman who brought freedom to a whole tribe is remembered at prayer, too.

how: Muslims honor Juwayriyyah bint al-Harith among the mothers of the believers, retelling from Sunan Abi Dawud how her marriage led to the freeing of her people, and many learn the words of remembrance taught to her in Sahih Muslim.

o: a chief's daughter whose marriage freed her people
a chief's daughter who led her tribe in battle
a captive who escaped back to her tribe by night

p: asked for help paying for her freedom
paid what she owed and married her
no woman a greater blessing to her people

s: the Prophet ordered the companions to free her people
in the report the companions freed them on their own, because they were now his in-laws.
Juwayriyyah came herself to ask for help
she went to the Prophet to ask for help with paying for her freedom.
the report says a hundred households were freed
Abu Dawud's report counts a hundred households of the Banu al-Mustaliq.

games.q: you are a companion holding captives from her tribe. you hear the Prophet has just married Juwayriyyah. what do you do?
o: keep them; nothing has been commanded.
free them, since they're now his in-laws.
ask the Prophet what he wants done.
games.why: the report says they freed them, saying the Prophet's in-laws should not be held captive.

practice: Think of someone near you carrying something they can't put down on their own: a chore that's swallowing them, an apology they're waiting for, a grudge you're holding against them, a worry nobody has helped with.
Pick the one you could lift, and see yourself lifting it. If you pray, ask to be a blessing to the people around you.

wordCard.voice: Juwayriyyah, the chief's daughter who asked the Prophet for help with her freedom, and whose marriage led the companions to free a hundred households. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: her name, Juwayriyyah bint al-Harith.

carryVoice: Your line: a blessing to her people. One brave question, and a hundred households walked out free. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 3931 (Juwayriyyah's request; the marriage; a hundred households freed; Aisha's words)
